t: Corinth, a Roman city in Greece
p: Rome destroyed old Corinth in 146 BC and refounded it as a colony in 44 BC. In Paul's day it was the capital of Achaia.
b: The Roman general Mummius sacked the old Greek city in 146 BC. Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 BC as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves, and it grew rich. It sat on the narrow isthmus between two seas, with a port on each side: Lechaeum to the west and Cenchreae to the east (18:18). Ships' cargo, and sometimes small ships, were hauled across the neck of land. Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games and was the seat of the Roman governor of Achaia (18:12). Its old reputation for sexual vice comes mostly from writers about the Greek city before 146 BC; Strabo's famous figure of a thousand temple prostitutes (Geography 8.6.20) describes that earlier city, and many historians doubt it. Paul's two letters to the church here show a mixed, quarrelsome, gifted congregation.

p: A Jewish couple from Rome who became Paul's coworkers. Priscilla is usually named first.
b: Aquila came from Pontus on the Black Sea coast of what is now Turkey; the couple had been living in Rome. Luke calls her Priscilla, a friendly form of the name; Paul calls her Prisca (Romans 16:3; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19). In four of the six places where both are named, she comes first (18:18, 26; Romans 16:3; 2 Timothy 4:19), which was unusual in the ancient world and may mean she was the better known or of higher rank. Luke never says they were converted by Paul, so they were probably believers already when they left Rome. They hosted churches in their home in Ephesus and later in Rome, and Paul says they risked their lives for him (Romans 16:4).

a: since Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome
t: Claudius expels the Jews from Rome
p: Suetonius says Claudius expelled Jews who rioted "at the prompting of Chrestus." Many think he means Christ.
b: The Roman historian Suetonius writes that Claudius "expelled from Rome the Jews, who were constantly making disturbances at the prompting of Chrestus" (Claudius 25.4). Chrestus was a common slave name, but Greeks and Romans often confused it with Christus, so many historians think the quarrels in Rome's synagogues were over Jesus as the Messiah. Others take Chrestus to be an otherwise unknown troublemaker. The Christian historian Orosius, writing about 417, dates the expulsion to Claudius' ninth year, AD 49, which fits Paul's arrival in Corinth about 50. Orosius names Josephus as his source, but no such passage is in Josephus' surviving works, which is one reason some scholars doubt his date. Cassius Dio says instead that Claudius, in AD 41, did not expel the Jews but banned their meetings (Roman History 60.6.6). Dio may describe an earlier step, or a milder version of the same event. Luke's "all the Jews" is probably a loose way of speaking, since Rome's Jewish community was large.

p: The Greek skēnopoioi means tentmakers. Tents were often leather, so Paul may have worked leather and canvas.
b: The word means "tent-makers." In the Roman world tents and awnings were made of leather or of woven goat's hair, so the trade probably covered both leatherwork and weaving. Ronald Hock argued that Paul worked in a shop, talking with customers as he worked, as some traveling philosophers did. Paul often says he worked with his own hands so as not to burden the churches (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 4:12; 9:6–18; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9), and he holds up his hands to the Ephesian elders as proof (20:34). Jewish teachers valued a trade alongside study: "study of the Torah together with a worldly occupation is excellent" (Mishnah Avot 2:2). The site translates the phrase literally; nothing in it means a missionary who supports himself, the modern sense of "tentmaker."

a: Once Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia
p: When Silas and Timothy arrived, they probably brought money from the Macedonian churches, freeing Paul to preach full time.
b: Paul had left Silas and Timothy in Macedonia (17:14–15). Paul's letters fill in the picture. Timothy came back from Thessalonica with good news, and Paul wrote 1 Thessalonians from Corinth in response (1 Thessalonians 3:6). Paul also says that believers who came from Macedonia supplied what he needed in Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:9), and the church at Philippi sent him gifts more than once (Philippians 4:15–16). So the change in this verse, from working at his trade on weekdays to being "taken up wholly with the word," most likely means the gifts let him stop making tents for a time. Paul's letters and Acts fit together closely here, one of several places where they can be checked against each other.

p: A public sign of breaking off: "I am finished here, and the responsibility is yours."
b: Shaking the dust off one's clothes or feet was a known gesture of separation. Jesus told his messengers to shake the dust from their feet against a town that would not hear them (Matthew 10:14; Luke 9:5), and Paul and Barnabas did so at Pisidian Antioch (13:51). Nehemiah shook out the fold of his robe as a sign of God shaking out anyone who broke an oath (Nehemiah 5:13). Here the gesture goes with words of responsibility (see the next note). It ends Paul's work in this synagogue, not his relationship with its people: he moves next door (18:7), and the synagogue's leader soon believes (18:8).

a: Your blood on your own head!
p: An Old Testament way of saying "you are responsible for what happens to you." It is not a curse.
b: The Greek has no verb: "Your blood on your head!" The formula comes from the Old Testament, where it fixes responsibility for a death: "Your blood is on your head" (2 Samuel 1:16); compare Joshua 2:19. Above all it recalls God's watchman in Ezekiel, who must warn the people; if he warns them and they do not listen, their blood is on their own heads and he is clear (Ezekiel 3:18–21; 33:1–9). Paul's "I am clean" means he has done his duty as a watchman. He uses the same picture again in his farewell at Miletus: "I am clean of everyone's blood" (20:26). The words are not a curse on the Jewish people. Christians have sometimes misread them, as they misread Matthew 27:25, but in the story Paul keeps visiting synagogues (18:19; 19:8).

a: From now on, I am going to the Gentiles
p: Paul's turn to the Gentiles here is local, not final. He goes straight back to synagogues in the next city.
b: Acts tells three scenes in which Paul announces that he is turning to the Gentiles: at Pisidian Antioch (13:46), here at Corinth, and at the very end in Rome (28:28). Readers have long argued over what they mean. Some take them as a growing rejection of the Jewish people as a whole, which reaches its final word in Rome; Jack Sanders read Luke-Acts this way. Others, such as Jacob Jervell, note that each turn is local. In Corinth Paul moves only next door (18:7), many Jews believe here and elsewhere (18:8; 21:20), and in the next city he goes first to the synagogue again (18:19; 19:8). On this reading, Acts tells of a divided Israel, not a rejected one. The question returns at 28:25–28.

p: A Gentile who attended the synagogue. His Roman name suggests a citizen of the colony. He may be the Gaius of Romans 16:23.
b: "Who worshiped God" is Luke's term for Gentiles who honored Israel's God and attended the synagogue without becoming full converts (13:43; 16:14; 17:4, 17). Titius is a Roman family name, so Justus was probably a Roman citizen of the colony. His house next to the synagogue became the church's meeting place, an awkward neighbor for the synagogue. Some scholars, following a suggestion of Edgar Goodspeed, identify him with Gaius, whom Paul baptized (1 Corinthians 1:14) and who hosted Paul and the whole church in Corinth (Romans 16:23): a Roman had three names, and "Gaius Titius Justus" would be a normal one. That is possible but unproven. The manuscripts spell the name three ways (see the variant).

p: The synagogue's leader believed. Paul names Crispus as one of the few people he baptized himself in Corinth.
b: The "leader of the synagogue" (Greek archisynagōgos) arranged the services and often paid for the building. A first-century inscription from Jerusalem names a certain Theodotus as priest and synagogue leader, who built a synagogue "for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments." Paul confirms this verse in passing: Crispus and Gaius were the only Corinthians he baptized himself (1 Corinthians 1:14). A synagogue leader joining Paul with his whole household was a serious blow to the community, and it helps explain the anger that leads to the hearing before Gallio. His successor may have been Sosthenes (18:17).

t: "Have no fear... for I am with you"
p: The Lord speaks to Paul in the words God used to encourage Israel and its prophets.
b: The vision borrows the language of God's promises in the Old Testament: "Don't be afraid, because I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and "Have no fear; I am with you" (Isaiah 43:5). God said much the same to Joshua (Joshua 1:9) and to Jeremiah when he was called (Jeremiah 1:8, 19). Paul is cast as a prophet called to speak to a hostile city. In his letter to this church Paul remembers that he came to them weak, afraid and trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3), which explains why he needed the vision. Acts gives him similar night visions at key moments (16:9; 23:11; 27:23–24).
r: Isaiah 41:10; Isaiah 43:5; Joshua 1:9; Jeremiah 1:8; 1 Corinthians 2:3; Acts 16:9; Acts 23:11; Acts 27:23–24

a: a large people in this city belongs to me
p: Laos, "people," is the Bible's usual word for Israel. Here the Lord uses it for the believers of Corinth, mostly Gentiles.
b: In the Greek Old Testament laos is the standard word for Israel as God's people. James uses it with surprise at the Jerusalem council: God has taken "a people for his name" from the Gentiles (15:14). Here the Lord says he already has a large "people" in Corinth, though most have not yet believed. Readers in the Reformed tradition (Calvin among them) have seen in this verse God's election of people who will come to faith later; others read it as God's foreknowledge of the coming harvest, or simply as a promise that the work will succeed. Either way, the word gives Gentile believers a title that once belonged to Israel, which is one of the main claims of Acts.

p: Eighteen months in Corinth, about AD 50 to 52, the longest Paul had stayed anywhere since he set out.
b: On his travels so far Paul had usually been driven out of a city within weeks (13:50; 14:6; 16:39; 17:10, 14). Here, under the Lord's promise, he stays a year and a half. With the Gallio inscription (see 18:12), this stay can be dated to roughly AD 50–52, one of the firmest dates in Paul's life. In this time he founded the church to which he later wrote at least two letters, and from here he wrote 1 Thessalonians, and probably 2 Thessalonians if he wrote it.

a: When Gallio was serving as proconsul of Achaia
t: Gallio and the inscription at Delphi
p: A letter of Claudius found at Delphi names Gallio proconsul, about AD 51–52. It anchors the dates of Paul's life.
b: Lucius Junius Gallio was the elder brother of the philosopher Seneca, Nero's tutor. Fragments of a stone inscription found at Delphi preserve a letter of the emperor Claudius that names "Gallio, my friend and proconsul." The letter is dated by Claudius' twenty-sixth acclamation as emperor, which fell in AD 52. Proconsuls of senatorial provinces served a one-year term that usually began in early summer, so Gallio most likely governed Achaia from mid-51 to mid-52 (a few scholars prefer 52–53). Seneca mentions that Gallio caught a fever in Achaia and left by ship (Moral Letters 104.1), which may mean he did not finish his term. Because Paul had already been in Corinth for some time when he stood before Gallio, this is the most important single date for the life of Paul.

p: A raised stone platform in the forum where the governor heard cases. Its remains are shown to visitors today.
b: The bēma was the platform from which a Roman official gave judgment in public. In the center of the forum at Corinth archaeologists uncovered a large raised platform faced with marble, usually identified as the bēma of this scene, though the identification is not certain and the remains may be slightly later. Paul uses the same word when he says that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10; Romans 14:10), a picture his Corinthian readers could see in their own forum.

a: in a way that goes against the law
p: The charge is vague on purpose. Gallio hears it as a dispute about Jewish law and refuses to rule on it.
b: The accusers may mean the law of Moses: Paul is teaching people to worship God without circumcision and the Jewish way of life. Or they may mean Roman law: Paul is spreading a new, unauthorized religion, which a governor could treat as a public danger (compare the charge at Philippi, 16:21). Later Christian writers such as Tertullian spoke of Judaism as a "permitted religion" (religio licita), but historians doubt that Rome had such a formal category in the first century. Gallio hears the case as an internal Jewish quarrel (18:15). For Luke's readers his ruling mattered: a senior Roman official saw the Christian message as a question within Judaism, not a crime against Rome, and so no reason to punish it.

a: I have no wish to be a judge of such matters
p: Roman governors had wide freedom to accept or turn away charges that did not fit Roman law.
b: Outside the fixed list of crimes, a provincial governor heard cases at his own discretion (in legal terms, cognitio extra ordinem). A. N. Sherwin-White showed how well this scene fits that practice: Gallio judges that the complaint is about "a word and names" and a law that is not Rome's, and he declines to act. "A word" may mean teaching, and "names" may be titles such as "Messiah." Other Roman officials in Acts say much the same (23:29; 25:18–20). Luke's readers learned from these scenes that Rome's own officers saw nothing criminal in the faith.

p: Luke does not say who "everyone" was. Greeks venting anger at Jews, or Jews angry at their failed leader?
b: The oldest manuscripts say only "everyone" (see the variant). Most readers think of the Greek bystanders, who took the chance to show their dislike of the Jewish accusers once the governor had sided against them; later copyists made this explicit by adding "the Greeks." Others suggest the Jews themselves turned on Sosthenes for losing the case, or because he too leaned toward Paul. A Sosthenes is named with Paul as co-sender of 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 1:1). If he is the same man, the leader who was beaten here later became a believer, like Crispus before him. The name was common, so this is possible, not certain.

a: None of these things mattered at all to Gallio
t: "Gallio cared for none of those things"
p: In the KJV this line became a proverb for religious indifference. In Luke it shows Roman neutrality.
b: The KJV's "Gallio cared for none of those things" became a common sermon text against people indifferent to religion, and "a Gallio" came to mean a careless person. In the story the point is different. Gallio is not a seeker who fails to care about the gospel; he is a judge who refuses to take sides in a religious dispute and will not stop a street beating that does not threaten order. For Luke's purpose, his indifference protects the church: Paul is free to stay "a good many days more" (18:18).
orig: οὐδὲν τούτων τῷ Γαλλίωνι ἔμελεν (ouden toutōn tō Galliōni emelen)

a: He had had his hair cut short at Cenchreae, for he was keeping a vow
p: The Greek does not make clear whether Paul or Aquila made the vow. Most think Paul, and that it was like a Nazirite vow.
b: The Greek participle "having cut his hair" comes right after "Priscilla and Aquila," so a few readers take Aquila as the one with the vow. Most commentators think Paul is meant, since he is the subject of the whole sentence. The vow resembles the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, during which the hair grew uncut; at the end, "the Nazirite will shave off the hair he dedicated" (Numbers 6:18). But that ending was done at the temple, and the Mishnah's tractate Nazir assumes Jerusalem for it, so this may have been a private vow of thanks, completed later in Jerusalem (18:21–22; see the spec box on this chapter). Either way, Luke shows Paul keeping Jewish custom of his own accord, as in 21:23–26 and 1 Corinthians 9:20.

p: The harbor on the Saronic Gulf, facing Asia. A church soon met here; its deacon Phoebe carried Paul's letter to Rome.
b: Cenchreae lay about seven miles (11 km) east of Corinth, on the gulf that opens toward the Aegean, so ships for Ephesus and Syria left from here. Remains of its harbor works are now under shallow water. A few years later there was a church at Cenchreae, and Paul commends Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae, to the Christians of Rome (Romans 16:1–2).

p: A common phrase among Greeks, Jews and Christians alike. James later warns believers to plan this way.
b: The phrase (literally "God willing it") was used in ordinary Greek letters and in Jewish speech. Paul uses forms of it in his letters (1 Corinthians 4:19; 16:7; Romans 1:10), and James tells believers to make their plans subject to the Lord's will (James 4:15). Paul did return to Ephesus (19:1) and stayed for over two years. The Byzantine text adds Paul's reason for leaving: he had to keep the coming feast in Jerusalem (see the variant).

a: he went up and paid his respects to the church
p: Luke does not name the city, but "going up" from the coast meant going up to Jerusalem.
b: Caesarea was a port, and the Greek says he "went up" and then "went down" to Antioch. In Jewish and biblical usage one always goes "up" to Jerusalem, so most interpreters take this as a short visit to the Jerusalem church, perhaps to fulfil the vow of 18:18. If so, it is Paul's fourth visit to Jerusalem in Acts (9:26; 11:30; 15:2; here; 21:15), told in one line. A few think he only greeted the church in Caesarea. The brevity suits Luke's story, which saves Jerusalem for the great final visit of chapters 21–23.

p: Paul revisits churches founded earlier. Where exactly "the Galatian country" was is debated.
b: Most English Bibles start Paul's "third missionary journey" here, but those numbered journeys are a modern way of dividing Acts; Luke does not count them. "The Galatian country and Phrygia" reverses the phrase at 16:6. Scholars debate whether Luke means the churches of the south of the Roman province of Galatia (Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch, chapters 13–14) or the ethnic Galatians farther north around Ancyra (modern Ankara). The answer affects which churches received Paul's letter to the Galatians and when. Paul may also have organized the collection for Jerusalem on this trip (1 Corinthians 16:1).

p: A gifted Jewish teacher from Egypt's great city. He later became a leader in Corinth, admired alongside Paul and Peter.
b: Alexandria had the largest Jewish community outside Judea and was a center of Greek learning; the Jewish philosopher Philo lived there and read Scripture with Greek tools of interpretation. The Greek Old Testament had also been made there. Apollos later worked in Corinth so effectively that some there claimed to belong to Apollos rather than to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6). Paul speaks of him warmly: Paul planted, and Apollos watered (1 Corinthians 3:6; 1 Corinthians 16:12; Titus 3:13). Martin Luther suggested that Apollos wrote the Letter to the Hebrews, with its polished Greek and close reading of Scripture. Many have found the guess attractive, but there is no early evidence for it.

p: The Greek logios can mean either a learned man or a skilled speaker. Both probably fit Apollos.
b: Logios comes from logos, "word," and in Greek of this time it could describe a person who was cultured and well read, or one who spoke well. English Bibles split between "eloquent" (KJV) and "learned." This translation keeps both ideas. Apollos' speaking skill seems to have mattered at Corinth, where Paul insisted that he himself had not come to them with fine speech or clever wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:1–4), perhaps with the contrast in mind.

t: Burning in spirit, or in the Spirit?
p: The Greek can describe Apollos' own zeal or the Holy Spirit's work in him. Paul uses the same phrase in Romans 12:11.
b: The phrase means literally "boiling in the spirit." Most translations take it of Apollos' own enthusiasm. Others read "aglow with the Spirit," since pneuma often means the Holy Spirit and Paul uses the same phrase in a list of exhortations that follows the gifts of grace (Romans 12:11). If the Spirit is meant, Apollos was a Spirit-filled believer whose knowledge of baptism was incomplete. If his own spirit is meant, he may still have been short of what 19:1–7 describes. Luke does not say Apollos was baptized again.

a: but the only baptism he knew was John's
t: A Christian who knew only John's baptism?
p: Apollos taught accurately about Jesus, yet knew only John's baptism. Interpreters explain this in several ways.
b: Luke says three positive things about Apollos (instructed in the way of the Lord, on fire, teaching accurately about Jesus) and one gap. Readings differ. (1) He learned the story of Jesus from followers of John the Baptist or from early disciples in Galilee or Alexandria, before Christian baptism in Jesus' name was known there; Priscilla and Aquila filled the gap, and his earlier baptism was let stand. (2) Ernst Käsemann argued that Luke tidies up history: both Apollos and the twelve men of 19:1–7 were really members of a rival movement around John, and Luke brings them under the apostolic church. (3) Luke contrasts the two cases on purpose: Apollos already had the Spirit and needed teaching, while the men of 19:1–7 lacked both.

a: laid out God's way for him more accurately
p: A woman, named first, teaches a learned man. The churches use this verse in their debate about women teaching.
b: Luke names Priscilla before her husband, and she shares in explaining "God's way" to a learned preacher. Some later copyists reversed the names (see the variant). John Chrysostom, preaching on Romans 16:3, praised Priscilla for instructing Apollos. In today's debate, egalitarian readers point to the verse as a woman teaching theology to a man, with Scripture's approval. Complementarian readers note that the teaching happened privately, in the couple's home and together with her husband, not in the church's gathering, and so it does not conflict with 1 Timothy 2:12. Both sides agree that Priscilla was a real teacher of the faith. The churches' cards on women in ministry are at Judges 4 and Proverbs 31; the main texts are in Paul's letters (1 Corinthians 14:34–35; 1 Timothy 2:11–15).

a: the brothers urged him on. They wrote to the disciples there to receive him
p: The first Christian letter of introduction we hear of. Travelers carried such letters from church to church.
b: In the ancient world a stranger arriving in a city needed someone to vouch for him. Christian churches wrote short letters commending their members to other congregations; Paul mentions them (2 Corinthians 3:1) and writes one himself for Phoebe (Romans 16:1–2). The Greek may mean that the Ephesian believers encouraged Apollos to go, or that they encouraged the Corinthians to welcome him; either way, the letter linked the believers at Ephesus with the church Paul had founded at Corinth.

t: Helped through grace, or believed through grace?
p: The phrase may say how Apollos helped (by God's gift) or how the Corinthians came to believe (by grace).
b: The Greek places "through grace" at the end of the sentence, after "those who had believed." It can go with "believed" (they had come to faith by God's grace, a Pauline idea, Ephesians 2:8) or with "helped" (Apollos was a great help by the grace God gave him, as in Romans 12:6). Translations divide. The Plain English Translation keeps the phrase between the two so the reader can see both.

a: he proved the Jews wrong, out in public
p: Luke uses a doubled compound found nowhere else in the New Testament: Apollos argued them down completely.
b: Diakatelenchomai stacks two prefixes on "refute": it means to argue someone down point by point. The debate was public and from "the Scriptures," which for both sides meant the Jewish Bible. The subject was the same as Paul's (18:5): whether the Messiah Israel awaited was Jesus. Luke presents this as an argument among Jews about their own Scriptures, not an attack on Jews from outside.

p: Paul took the higher inland route west to Ephesus. Codex Bezae adds that the Spirit sent him back to Asia.
b: From the Galatian and Phrygian country (18:23), the main road to Ephesus ran down the Lycus and Maeander valleys. "The upper parts" suggests Paul took a higher route over the hills to the north, which may be why he did not visit Colossae and Laodicea, whose churches had never seen him (Colossians 2:1). The papyrus P38 (about 300), Codex Bezae (05, about 400) and the margin of the Harclean Syriac, witnesses of the Western text, open the chapter differently: Paul wanted to go to Jerusalem by his own plan, but the Spirit told him to return to Asia (reported by Metzger; see the variant). The addition explains how 18:21 was fulfilled and stresses the Spirit's guidance, as 16:6–7 does.

t: Ephesus, the leading city of Asia
p: A great port, home of the temple of Artemis and the Roman governor of Asia. Paul's base for more than two years.
b: Ephesus stood near the mouth of the Cayster River on the Aegean coast of what is now Turkey. It was one of the largest cities of the eastern empire (estimates of its population range widely, from about 100,000 to over 200,000) and the seat of the proconsul of Asia. Its temple of Artemis was counted among the seven wonders of the world. Roads and sea lanes made it a hub for the whole province, which is why Paul could stay put and still reach "everyone living in Asia" (19:10). Ephesus later appears in Revelation 2:1–7, in a letter that bears Paul's name (Ephesians 1:1), and in the letters of Ignatius about AD 110.

p: Luke calls them disciples, his usual word for Christians, yet they have not heard of the Spirit. Views differ.
b: Everywhere else in Acts "disciples" means followers of Jesus, and Luke does not call them "disciples of John." Yet they know only John's baptism and have not received the Spirit. Interpreters read them in three main ways. (1) They were believers in Jesus whose instruction stopped short, like Apollos (18:25), and Paul completes it. (2) They were followers of John the Baptist, a movement that outlived him (Luke 7:18; 11:1; John 3:25–26), and Luke calls them "disciples" loosely; Käsemann thought Luke was absorbing that movement into the church. (3) James Dunn argued that Paul's question exposes that they were not yet Christians at all, since in the New Testament someone without the Spirit does not belong to Christ (Romans 8:9). The churches' answers also differ: see the card at Acts 2:4 on a second experience of the Spirit, and the card below on rebaptism.

a: When you came to believe, did you receive the Holy Spirit?
p: The KJV's "since ye believed" suggested a second experience after faith. The Greek more naturally means "when."
b: Paul's question uses an aorist participle, pisteusantes, "having believed," with an aorist main verb, "did you receive." In such pairs the participle usually describes an action at the same time as the main verb: "did you receive the Spirit when you believed?" The KJV's "since ye believed" was read in the Holiness movement and early Pentecostalism as pointing to a later experience after conversion, and the verse became a key text for that teaching. Grammar alone cannot settle the matter, since the participle can also mean "after you believed." But Paul's follow-up question, "Then into what were you baptized?", assumes that believing, baptism and the Spirit normally come together. The card at Acts 2:4 sets out how the churches differ on a second experience of the Spirit after faith, with tongues as its sign; this site gives that question one card, at its first occurrence.
orig: Εἰ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐλάβετε πιστεύσαντες; (Ei pneuma hagion elabete pisteusantes?)

a: we never even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit
t: Never heard of the Holy Spirit?
p: Followers of John knew the Spirit from Scripture and from John's own words. They probably mean the Spirit had not yet come.
b: Anyone taught by John the Baptist would have heard him promise one who "will baptize you in the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 3:11; compare Luke 3:16), and the Spirit appears throughout Israel's Scriptures. So most interpreters take the answer to mean "we have not even heard that the Holy Spirit has been given." John's Gospel uses the same short expression: literally "the Spirit was not yet," which this site renders "the Spirit had not yet come" (John 7:39). These men had heard John's promise but not the news of its fulfillment at Pentecost.
orig: οὐδ’ εἰ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἔστιν (oud’ ei pneuma hagion estin)

p: John's washing was a sign of repentance before the coming of the one who would bring the Spirit.
b: John the Baptist called Israel to repent and be baptized in the Jordan as they waited for the one coming after him (Luke 3:3–17). Josephus also describes John as a good man who urged Jews to practice justice and devotion to God and so to come to baptism, which he says served to purify the body when the soul had already been cleansed by right living (Antiquities 18.116–119). Christians later understood John's baptism as preparing the way, while baptism "into the name of the Lord Jesus" brought people into belonging to Jesus and was tied to the gift of the Spirit (2:38).

p: Paul sums up John's preaching in John's own words, as the Gospels and Paul's sermon at Antioch give them.
b: John said: "But the one coming after me is stronger than I am" (Matthew 3:11). Paul quoted the same saying in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (13:25). Here Paul simply finishes John's thought: the one John pointed to is Jesus. This is the heart of Luke's picture of John the Baptist throughout Luke-Acts: a true prophet whose whole work pointed beyond himself.

a: they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus
t: "Into the name of the Lord Jesus"
p: The only clear case of people baptized twice in the New Testament. "Into the name" means into belonging to Jesus.
b: Acts describes Christian baptism as "in" or "into the name of Jesus Christ" or "the Lord Jesus" (2:38; 8:16; 10:48), while Matthew 28:19 has "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Many scholars think Acts describes what kind of baptism it was (into Jesus' ownership and service), not the exact words spoken, though early practice may have varied; the Didache, about AD 100, gives the threefold name (Didache 7:1) but also speaks of those "baptized into the name of the Lord" (Didache 9:5). Calvin denied that these men were baptized again in water: he took "baptized" here to mean the gift of the Spirit given by laying on of hands (Institutes 4.15.18). Other Protestant interpreters since the Reformation have read verse 5 as the end of Paul's own sentence: John's hearers, on hearing John, were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus, so that no second baptism is narrated at all. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take it as a water baptism given by Paul. See the card below.
orig: ἐβαπτίσθησαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ (ebaptisthēsan eis to onoma tou kyriou Iēsou)

a: Then Paul laid hands on them
p: A gesture of blessing, commissioning and prayer. Here, as in Samaria, the Spirit comes through it.
b: Laying hands on someone goes back to Israel's rites of blessing and commissioning (Genesis 48:14; Numbers 27:18–23). In Acts it accompanies healing (9:12, 17; 28:8), sending out for a task (6:6; 13:3), and the gift of the Spirit (8:17; here). Hebrews 6:2 lists "laying on of hands" among the church's basic teachings. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches see in this verse, with 8:14–17, the roots of confirmation or chrismation; others read it as an event that belongs to the first spread of the gospel. The question of what this scene means for believers now is on the card at Acts 2:4; the card at 8:14–17 covers confirmation.

a: They began to speak in tongues and to prophesy
p: The third time Acts shows the Spirit arriving with speech: Jerusalem, Caesarea and now Ephesus.
b: Luke tells three scenes where the Spirit comes on a new group with visible signs of speech: the Jewish disciples at Pentecost (2:4), the Gentiles in Cornelius' house (10:46), and these followers of John (here). Each marks a new stage in the spread of the gospel (1:8). Prophesying recalls Moses' elders, who "prophesied" when the spirit settled on them (Numbers 11:25), and Joel's promise quoted at Pentecost (2:17–18). Whether "tongues" here are known languages, as at Pentecost (2:6–11), or the inspired speech Paul discusses in 1 Corinthians 12–14, Luke does not say. Paul wrote his own account of tongues in 1 Corinthians during this same stay in this city (1 Corinthians 16:8).

p: Twelve recalls Israel's tribes and the Twelve apostles, but Luke's "about" warns against pressing the number.
b: Some readers see in the twelve men a renewed Israel in miniature, the core of a new church in Asia, as the Twelve were in Jerusalem. Luke's word "about" makes the number look like a plain count, not a symbol. Still, the scene does stand at the start of Paul's longest work in one city, and the twelve are the first church in Ephesus that Luke describes.

p: One of the earliest names the movement used for itself. It may echo Isaiah's call to clear "the way of the LORD."
b: Before they were called "Christians" (11:26), believers called their movement "the Way" (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). The name probably comes from Isaiah: "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3), the verse the Gospels connect with John the Baptist (Luke 3:4). The Jewish community at Qumran used the same verse for itself and called its life "the way" (Community Rule, 1QS 8:13–16; 9:17–20). The name also points to a manner of life, not just a set of beliefs. It shows the early believers thinking of themselves inside Israel's hope, as one Jewish group among others (24:14).

p: A lecture hall, perhaps owned by or named for a teacher called Tyrannus. Paul taught there daily for two years.
b: The Greek scholē first meant "leisure," then a place where people spent leisure in discussion, and so a lecture hall. Tyrannus may have been the teacher who used it or the owner who rented it out. Teaching daily in such a hall, Paul would have looked to outsiders like a traveling philosopher with his students. The Western text adds the hours he used it, "from the fifth hour to the tenth," that is, about 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. (see the variant). If that tradition is right, Paul worked at his trade in the cool early morning (20:34) and taught through the midday break when the hall stood empty.

t: How the gospel spread through Asia
p: Paul stayed in Ephesus while his coworkers carried the message to nearby cities such as Colossae and Laodicea.
b: "Everyone" is a happy exaggeration, but the claim fits what Paul's letters show. Epaphras, from Colossae, founded churches there and in Laodicea and Hierapolis, cities Paul himself never visited (Colossians 1:7; 2:1; 4:12–13). Several of the seven churches in Revelation 2–3 probably go back to this period. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, speaking of a wide door opened for him and many opponents (1 Corinthians 16:8–9), and he mentions troubles in Asia so severe that he despaired of life (2 Corinthians 1:8–10). Many scholars think he was imprisoned in Ephesus at some point, and that Philippians or Philemon may have been written there, though Luke says nothing of it.
r: 20:31; 1 Corinthians 16:8–9; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8–10; Colossians 1:7; Colossians 4:12–13; Revelation 1:11

a: Sweat cloths or work aprons from his skin
p: Cloths that had touched Paul's skin healed the sick. Readers have drawn very different lessons from this.
b: The two Greek words come from Latin: soudarion (Latin sudarium) was a sweat-rag or handkerchief, and simikinthion (Latin semicinctium) a work apron, the gear of Paul's trade (18:3). Luke tells similar stories of Jesus' clothes (Luke 8:44) and Peter's shadow (5:15), and stresses that God was the one acting (19:11). Catholic and Orthodox Christians have seen here a biblical basis for honoring the relics of saints (compare 2 Kings 13:21, where the card on relics is). Some Pentecostal and healing ministries send out "prayer cloths" citing this verse. Many Protestants treat the scene as an "extraordinary" sign tied to the apostles' founding work, not a pattern. Luke places it just before a story about people who tried to use Jesus' name like a magic word (19:13–16), which suggests he saw the danger of treating such things as magic.

t: Jewish exorcists and the name of Jesus
p: Exorcism was a known trade. Magical texts of the time even call on "Jesus, the god of the Hebrews."
b: Jews had a reputation in the ancient world for powerful exorcisms. Josephus tells of a Jew named Eleazar who drew a demon out of a man before the future emperor Vespasian using a ring and incantations said to come from Solomon (Antiquities 8.45–49). Jesus himself mentions Jewish exorcists: "with whose help do your own sons throw them out?" (Matthew 12:27). Names of powerful figures were collected and used in spells; a long Greek magical papyrus from Egypt, now in Paris, includes the line "I adjure you by the god of the Hebrews, Jesus" (Greek Magical Papyri IV.3019–3020). These men treat Jesus' name the same way, as a borrowed formula: "the Jesus Paul preaches." Compare Mark 9:38–40, where someone outside the disciples casts out demons in Jesus' name and Jesus does not stop him.

p: No high priest named Sceva is known. Luke may be repeating his own claim, or the title may be loose.
b: Josephus' lists of the high priests from Herod to the war with Rome have no Sceva. Several explanations are offered. "High priest" in Acts can mean a member of the high-priestly families (4:6), and Sceva may have belonged to one. Or he may have claimed the title for himself, since a high priest, who alone spoke God's name in the temple, would carry great prestige among people who dealt in names of power. Or Luke is being ironic. Codex Bezae tells the scene differently and calls Sceva only "a priest" (reported by Metzger).

a: I know Jesus, and I am acquainted with Paul. But you, who are you?
p: The spirit uses two different verbs: it knows Jesus, and it is aware of Paul. The exorcists it does not know at all.
b: The first verb, ginōskō, is the ordinary word for knowing a person; the second, epistamai, means to know about or be acquainted with. English Bibles often blur the difference ("Jesus I know, and Paul I know"). The Gospels show unclean spirits recognizing Jesus at once (Luke 4:34, 41; 8:28). The scene is grimly funny: the borrowed name does not work for people who do not belong to the one who bears it. Compare Jesus' warning about those who used his name without knowing him (Matthew 7:22–23).
orig: τὸν Ἰησοῦν γινώσκω καὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι (ton Iēsoun ginōskō kai ton Paulon epistamai)

a: They fled out of that house stripped and wounded
p: The would-be exorcists flee naked: shame instead of power, a story told with clear humor.
b: Being stripped was the deepest public shame. Readers of Luke's Gospel may remember the man possessed by many demons who wore no clothes until Jesus freed him (Luke 8:27, 35); here the roles are reversed, and the exorcists end up naked. The Greek word behind "them all" literally means "both" (see the variant), which has led some to think only two of the seven brothers were present that day.

a: openly admitting and reporting their practices
p: The word praxeis can mean magic spells. Believers were giving away the secret formulas that made spells work.
b: Praxis means "deed," but in Greek magical texts it is also a technical word for a spell or magical procedure, and many scholars think that sense is meant here. Magic was thought to work only while its formulas stayed secret, so disclosing them was a way of giving up their power. The people coming forward "had come to faith" already, a reminder that converts did not leave old habits all at once. Their openness leads to the public burning in the next verse.

a: the total was fifty thousand silver coins
t: Books of magic, burned in public
p: Ephesus was famous for magic. The books burned were worth about fifty thousand days' wages.
b: Ancient writers spoke of "Ephesian letters" (Ephesia grammata), strings of mysterious words used as charms; Clement of Alexandria lists some of them (Stromata 5.8). Many magical handbooks from this period survive on papyrus from Egypt, full of names of gods, angels and Hebrew-sounding words. The "silver coins" were probably drachmas, each about a day's pay for a laborer (compare Matthew 20:2, where the denarius is a day's wage). Burning books in public was a known way to reject a teaching. Luke tells the story to show the Lord's power overcoming the magic for which Ephesus was known (19:20).

p: One of Luke's summary statements that close the main sections of Acts.
b: Luke marks the stages of Acts with short reports that "the word of God grew" (6:7; 12:24; compare 9:31; 16:5; 28:31). This is the last of them before the story turns toward Jerusalem and Rome (19:21). The Greek word order is unusual: in the critical text, "by the might of the Lord" comes first, which can be read "mightily the word of the Lord grew" or "by the Lord's might the word grew." The Byzantine text puts "the word of the Lord" together (see the variant). Either way, the point is that the word grows by God's strength, in a city of magic and powerful spirits.

t: His own spirit, or the Holy Spirit?
p: Paul "set in spirit" to go to Jerusalem. The phrase may mean he resolved in his mind, or that the Holy Spirit led him.
b: The idiom "to set in the spirit" can mean simply "to make up one's mind" (compare Luke 1:66; 21:14, "set in your heart"). But Luke so often says the Holy Spirit guided Paul (13:2–4; 16:6–7; 20:22–23) that many read it as "in the Spirit." The Plain English Translation keeps a capital S with that reading in mind, and 20:22 says Paul goes to Jerusalem "bound in the Spirit."
orig: ἔθετο ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῷ πνεύματι (etheto ho Paulos en tō pneumati)

a: I must see Rome as well
p: Luke's "must" marks God's plan. From here Acts heads for Jerusalem and Rome, as Luke's Gospel heads for Jerusalem.
b: Luke uses "must" (dei) for what God has planned: the Son of Man must suffer (Luke 9:22), and Paul "must bear witness in Rome too" (23:11) and stand before Caesar (27:24). This verse sets the course of the rest of the book, just as Luke 9:51 sets the course of the Gospel when Jesus resolutely turns toward Jerusalem. Paul's journey will echo Jesus': a determined journey to Jerusalem, warnings of suffering, arrest, and trials before Jewish and Roman rulers. In his letter to the Romans, written a few months later, Paul says the same plan in his own words (Romans 1:10–15; 15:22–29).

p: Paul's helper Erastus may be the Corinthian city treasurer of Romans 16:23. A paving stone in Corinth names an Erastus.
b: Three New Testament texts name an Erastus: Paul's helper here, Erastus the city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23), and an Erastus who stayed behind in Corinth (2 Timothy 4:20). In 1929 archaeologists in Corinth found a paving stone with a Latin inscription: "Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid [this pavement] at his own expense." An aedile was a city magistrate in charge of streets and markets. Whether this is the Erastus of Romans 16:23, and whether a treasurer could become an aedile, is debated; the date of the inscription is also disputed. If the identification holds, Paul's circle included a man of high civic rank. Whether the helper sent to Macedonia is the same man is uncertain.

p: Small models of the goddess's temple or shrine, sold to pilgrims. Clay and stone ones survive; silver ones have not.
b: The Greek says Demetrius made "silver shrines (naoi) of Artemis," which probably means small models of the goddess in her shrine, bought by pilgrims as offerings or keepsakes. Small terracotta and marble shrines of the mother goddess have been found in the region, but no silver one of this kind has come to light, which is not surprising for objects that could be melted down. An inscription of AD 104 records the gift of a rich Roman, Gaius Vibius Salutaris, of gold and silver images of Artemis and other figures, to be carried through the streets and set up in the theater at assemblies and festivals. It shows how closely the city's civic life, its theater (19:29) and its silver goddess were bound together.

p: Not the huntress of Greek myth (the KJV's Diana), but a great mother goddess of Asia, worshiped across the world.
b: The KJV calls her "Diana," her Roman name. The Artemis of Ephesus was quite different from the slender Greek hunter. Her statues show a stiff figure covered on the chest with rows of rounded objects, read variously as breasts, eggs, bull's testicles from sacrifices, or ornaments; scholars do not agree. Her temple, the Artemision, was about four times the size of the Parthenon. It burned in 356 BC and was rebuilt even more grandly. It was a bank, a place of refuge, and the center of a great festival economy. Pausanias says that all cities worshiped Artemis of Ephesus (Description of Greece 4.31.8). The honest verdict: Luke is describing real worship, at a real temple whose ruins remain, and the crowd's fear for its goddess's "greatness" (19:27) was real.

a: our good living comes out of this work
p: As at Philippi, the trouble begins when the gospel threatens someone's income.
b: At Philippi a slave girl's owners dragged Paul to the authorities when "their hope of income had gone out with it" (16:19). Here the craftsmen's livelihood is at stake. Luke's Gospel often warns about money as a rival god (Luke 12:15; 16:13). Demetrius' speech is a skilled piece of persuasion: he starts with income, moves to the honor of the city and its temple, and ends with the goddess's worldwide fame (19:27).

a: He says that gods produced by hands are not gods
p: Paul's message is the old Jewish teaching against idols, from the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets.
b: Israel's Scriptures mock gods "made by human hands, wood and stone" (Deuteronomy 4:28) and say: "Their idols are silver and gold, / something human hands have made" (Psalm 115:4; compare Psalm 135:15; Isaiah 44:9–20). Paul said the same in Athens (17:24–29) and wrote it to Gentile converts: they had turned from idols to God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Demetrius is a fair witness to Paul's teaching, even if he exaggerates its reach. The words "made by hands" are also used in Acts for the temple (7:48; 17:24).

p: A theater for about 20,000 to 25,000 people, still standing, where the city's assembly met.
b: The theater, cut into the slope of Mount Pion at the end of a grand street running from the harbor, could seat perhaps 20,000 to 25,000 people; it was rebuilt and enlarged during the first century. Greek cities held their formal assemblies (ekklēsiai) in such theaters, so a crowd rushing there was, in effect, calling an unofficial assembly (see 19:39). Visitors can still sit in it today. Gaius and Aristarchus appear again as Paul's companions (20:4; 27:2; Colossians 4:10, where Aristarchus is Paul's fellow prisoner).

p: Leading men of the province, tied to its assembly and to the cult of the emperor. Some were on friendly terms with Paul.
b: Inscriptions name many Asiarchs, wealthy men who held honored posts in the province of Asia. Scholars debate whether the title meant the high priests of the provincial temples of the emperor (Steven Friesen and others) or a broader group of leading citizens who paid for festivals and games. Either way, these were the province's elite. Luke's note that some of them were Paul's friends and protected him is pointed: the people closest to Rome's power in Asia saw no threat in Paul. The detail is also one that critics of Acts have found hard to explain as invention, since the title was local and specific.

p: The word Luke uses for the city assembly is the same one he uses for the church. This translation keeps "assembly" here.
b: In Greek cities the ekklēsia was the assembly of citizens called together to decide public business. Christians took the same word, by way of the Greek Old Testament's "assembly" of Israel, for their own gatherings: "the church." This site renders it "assembly" in 19:32, 39 and 41, where the city meeting is meant, and "church" for the Christian community. Luke may intend the contrast: the city's assembly is in a muddle and does not know why it has met (19:32), while in the next chapter Paul speaks to the leaders of "the church of God" (20:17, 28).

a: since the Jews were pushing him to the front
t: Alexander and the Jews of Ephesus
p: The Jewish community tries to separate itself from Paul. The crowd, seeing only a Jew, will not listen.
b: Ephesus had an old Jewish community whose rights, such as keeping the Sabbath and sending money to the temple, were confirmed by Roman decrees that Josephus preserves (Antiquities 14.223–227, 262–264; 16.167–168). Jews too rejected idols, so a riot against Paul's anti-idol preaching was dangerous for them. They push Alexander forward, probably to explain that the Jewish community was not to blame. But the crowd hears only that he is a Jew and drowns him out for two hours. The scene shows how quickly a Greek city could turn on its Jews. An "Alexander the coppersmith" who did Paul harm (2 Timothy 4:14; compare 1 Timothy 1:20) may or may not be the same man; the name was very common.

p: The highest civic official of the city. He answered to the Roman governor for public order.
b: The "clerk of the people" (grammateus tou dēmou) is well known from Ephesian inscriptions. He prepared the business of the assembly, published its decrees, and dealt with the Roman authorities, so a riot was his problem. (The same Greek word is the Gospels' "scribes" for experts in the law of Moses, but here it is a Greek civic office.) His speech is a model of calming a crowd: he flatters the city (19:35), states what all agree on (19:36), clears the accused (19:37), points to the proper courts (19:38–39), and ends with the real danger, Rome (19:40).

a: the temple warden of the great Artemis, and of what fell from the sky
t: Temple warden, and the thing that fell from the sky
p: Neōkoros, "temple warden," was a proud civic title. The "thing fallen from the sky" was a sacred image or stone.
b: A neōkoros was literally a temple sweeper, but cities used the word as an honor title: "warden" of a great temple. Inscriptions call Ephesus neōkoros of Artemis, and later of temples of the emperors. The clerk's last words name an object "fallen from Zeus" or "from the sky" (diopetēs). Greeks told of sacred images that fell from heaven; Euripides' play Iphigenia among the Taurians centers on such an image of Artemis. Some suggest a meteorite was kept in the temple. The Greek does not say "image" or "stone," so the Plain English Translation keeps it open: "what fell from the sky."

p: Paul's team preached against idols without attacking temples or mocking the goddess. Jewish teaching forbade both.
b: Temple robbery was a serious crime, and Jews were sometimes accused of it by their enemies. Josephus says that Moses forbade Jews to insult the gods of other peoples or to rob foreign temples (Antiquities 4.207; Against Apion 2.237), and Paul himself asks whether those who detest idols rob temples (Romans 2:22). The clerk's statement suggests that Paul argued against idols in general terms (19:26) but did not insult Artemis by name or encourage attacks on her temple.

a: court days are held and there are proconsuls
p: Each province had one proconsul. The plural may be a general statement, or a clue to a moment in AD 54.
b: The clerk speaks of "proconsuls" in the plural, though Asia had only one at a time. Most take it as a general plural ("there are such things as proconsuls"). Some scholars connect it with a specific moment: in late AD 54 the proconsul of Asia, Junius Silanus, was poisoned at the order of Nero's mother Agrippina by two imperial agents, Celer and Helius, who then ran the province's affairs for a time (Tacitus, Annals 13.1). If so, the riot would date to that winter. The theory is attractive but cannot be proved.

p: An unlawful assembly could bring Roman punishment on the whole city. The clerk's real fear is Rome.
b: Rome allowed Greek cities to govern themselves as long as they kept order. Riots could cost a city its privileges: after a deadly riot in the amphitheater of Pompeii in AD 59, the Senate banned games there for ten years and dissolved illegal clubs (Tacitus, Annals 14.17). The clerk's word stasis, "uprising," was the term for civil strife or rebellion, the same charge later brought against Paul (24:5). Luke's readers see the irony: the people who accused the Christians of disturbing the peace are the ones in danger of being charged with it.

a: Having said this, he sent the assembly home
p: Most Greek editions print these words as the end of verse 40. The KJV numbering makes them verse 41.
b: The chapter and verse numbers were added long after Acts was written: verses were numbered by Robert Estienne (Stephanus) in his Greek New Testament of 1551. Most modern Greek editions, including the SBL and NA28, print "and having said this he dismissed the assembly" as the last sentence of verse 40, so Acts 19 has forty verses in them and forty-one in the KJV and most English Bibles. Nothing is missing or added; the same words are simply numbered differently. This site follows the English numbering.
orig: καὶ ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἀπέλυσεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν (kai tauta eipōn apelysen tēn ekklēsian)

t: Months that Paul's letters fill in
p: Luke covers about a year in three verses. Paul's letters to Corinth and Rome tell much more about it.
b: Luke is brief here, but 2 Corinthians shows what these months were like. Paul went to Troas and, finding no rest because Titus had not come, went on to Macedonia, where Titus brought news from Corinth (2 Corinthians 2:12–13; 7:5–7). He wrote 2 Corinthians in Macedonia, gathering the collection for the poor in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8–9). He may also have gone as far as Illyricum, on the Adriatic (Romans 15:19). Then he spent three months in "Greece," almost certainly in Corinth, where he wrote his letter to the Romans (Romans 15:25–26; 16:1, 23).
r: 2 Corinthians 2:12–13; 2 Corinthians 7:5–7; 2 Corinthians 8:1–9:15; Romans 15:19; Romans 15:25–26; Romans 16:1; Romans 16:23

a: the Jews laid a plot against him
p: Some of Corinth's Jews planned to attack Paul as he sailed. Luke names the group loosely as "the Jews."
b: Paul had probably planned to sail with Jewish pilgrims going to Jerusalem for Passover. On a crowded pilgrim ship it would have been easy to harm him and the money he carried for the Jerusalem church. So he changed his route and went overland through Macedonia. Luke says "the Jews" here, as he often does for a particular group of Jewish opponents in a given city; the same chapter has Paul still appealing to "Jews and Greeks alike" (20:21), and he is hurrying to Jerusalem for a Jewish feast (20:16). Paul himself feared trouble from unbelievers in Judea on this journey (Romans 15:31).

t: The delegates and the missing collection
p: These men came from the churches Paul founded. Paul's letters show they were carrying a gift of money to Jerusalem.
b: The list names men from Macedonia (Berea, Thessalonica), Galatia (Derbe), and Asia. Paul's letters explain why: he had organized a large collection from his Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem, and he wanted the churches to send their own delegates with it (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8:16–24; Romans 15:25–28). Luke barely mentions this collection; only in 24:17 does Paul say he came "to give alms for my people." Scholars give different reasons for Luke's silence: the gift may have been refused or received coldly in Jerusalem (Paul feared this, Romans 15:31), it may have looked like a political act, or Luke may have had other aims. Sopater may be the Sosipater of Romans 16:21; Tychicus later carried letters (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7); Trophimus is the man whose presence with Paul sparks the riot in the temple (21:29).
r: 24:17; 21:29; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8:16–24; Romans 15:25–31; Romans 16:21; Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7

a: were waiting for us in Troas
p: The narrator says "we" again, for the first time since Philippi in chapter 16. What does it mean?
b: Acts switches from "they" to "we" in three stretches of travel: 16:10–17, 20:5–21:18, and 27:1–28:16. The last "we" was at Philippi (16:17), and it starts again at Philippi now (20:6). Views: (1) the author was there, and the "we" marks his own presence, as Irenaeus already understood and as many scholars still hold; (2) the author used a travel diary kept by a companion of Paul and kept its "we"; (3) "we" is a literary device, perhaps a convention of sea-voyage stories (Vernon Robbins), meant to give vividness and authority. Against the third view, the "we" is not limited to sea travel and drops out at odd points. The precise, day-by-day log of this voyage (20:6, 13–15) reads like a diary.

t: Paul keeps time by the Jewish feasts
p: Luke dates the journey by Passover week and Pentecost, as a Jew would, even in a Gentile city.
b: Luke marks this journey by the Jewish calendar: Paul leaves Philippi after the week of Unleavened Bread, which follows Passover, and hurries to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, fifty days later (20:16). Whether Paul kept the feast in Philippi with the believers or only timed his travel by it, the detail shows that the Jewish year still shaped Paul's life and probably that of his churches (compare 1 Corinthians 5:7–8). Luke also seems to shape Paul's journey to Jerusalem around a Passover, as Jesus' last journey was.

a: On the first day of the week
t: Meeting on the first day of the week
p: The first clear report of Christians gathering on Sunday. Whether it was Saturday night or Sunday night is debated.
b: The phrase is the one the Gospels use for the day of the resurrection (Matthew 28:1; John 20:1, 19). Paul tells the Corinthians to set money aside on the first day of each week (1 Corinthians 16:2), and John was in the Spirit "on the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10). Writers soon after the New Testament speak plainly of Sunday worship (Didache 14:1; Ignatius, To the Magnesians 9:1; Justin, First Apology 67). If Luke counts days the Jewish way, from sunset, this meeting began on Saturday evening; if the Roman way, on Sunday evening. Either way it was a night meeting, since many believers worked during the day. On whether this changes the Sabbath, see the cards at Revelation 1 and Matthew 12; on how often to break bread, the card below.

t: "To break bread": a meal and the Lord's Supper
p: Breaking bread was the reason for the meeting. Most readers think it included the Lord's Supper.
b: "Breaking bread" can mean any meal begun with the Jewish blessing over bread. But Luke uses it for the meals of the first church (2:42, 46), for the risen Jesus' meal at Emmaus (Luke 24:30, 35), and Paul speaks of the bread that believers break as a sharing in Christ's body (1 Corinthians 10:16). That believers gathered on the first day "to break bread" suggests a regular meal at which they kept the Lord's Supper, as Paul describes at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:20–26). In 20:11 Paul "broke the bread" and "had something to eat," which may mean the Supper and the meal together. The verse is used today as an argument for weekly communion (see the card).

p: An eyewitness detail, and perhaps the reason the young man grew drowsy. Some think it also answers a rumor.
b: The oil lamps would have made the crowded upper room hot and stuffy late at night, which helps explain why Eutychus fell asleep. The detail sounds like the memory of someone who was there (the "we" of 20:7). Some scholars also suggest that Luke is quietly answering slander: pagan critics later claimed that Christians met at night in darkness for shameful acts, a charge the Christian writer Minucius Felix reports and refutes (Octavius 9). Here the room is full of light. That second reading is possible but cannot be proved.

p: Eutychus means "fortunate." The name was common, especially among slaves, but here it fits the story.
b: Eutychos means "lucky" or "fortunate," a common name, often given to slaves. A young man who falls from the third story and lives is fortunate indeed, though Luke credits his life to God, not luck. Luke calls him a neanias, "young man" (20:9), and then a pais, "boy" (20:12), perhaps a teenager or a young slave. City apartment blocks of several floors were common in the Roman world; the upper rooms were often cheaper and less safe.

p: Luke says plainly he was "lifted up dead." Some readers think he only seemed dead.
b: The Greek says he "was taken up dead," not "as if dead." Most commentators, ancient and modern, read the story as a raising from the dead, like Peter's raising of Tabitha (9:36–42), so that Paul matches Peter and both match Elijah and Elisha. Others point to Paul's words, "his life is still in him" (20:10), and think Eutychus was unconscious and only appeared dead. Paul's words can also mean that life had already come back as he embraced him. Luke's description of the people's great comfort (20:12) suits a return from death.

a: fell on him and wrapped his arms around him
p: Paul stretches himself over the young man, as Elijah and Elisha did over dead boys.
b: Elijah "lay stretched out full length on top of the boy" three times and prayed (1 Kings 17:21). Elisha "climbed up and lay down on the child" until the boy's flesh grew warm (2 Kings 4:34). Paul's action recalls both, and the boy, like theirs, is given back alive. Paul's "Stop the commotion" uses the same Greek verb as Jesus' question to the mourners at Jairus' house, asking why they were making a commotion (Mark 5:39). Luke builds these parallels so that the reader sees the same God at work through the prophets, through Jesus, through Peter (9:40) and through Paul.

a: since he meant to make the trip on foot himself
p: About twenty miles (30 km) by road, while the ship went the long way around the cape. Luke gives no reason.
b: The coastal road from Troas to Assos was about 20 miles (30 km); the ship had to sail around Cape Lectum, a longer and often windy route. Luke does not say why Paul chose to walk. He may have wanted time alone before Jerusalem, or a last visit to believers along the way, or simply to avoid a rough passage. Assos had a fine harbor on the Gulf of Adramyttium, facing the island of Lesbos, where Mitylene was its main city (20:14).

t: Miletus and the "place of the Jews"
p: An old Greek city south of Ephesus. A seat in its theater was marked for "Jews who are also God-fearers."
b: Miletus, about 30 miles (50 km) south of Ephesus by sea, was once one of the greatest Greek cities, home of early philosophers. By Paul's time its harbor was silting up. An inscription carved on a row of seats in its theater reads, in one common translation, "Place of the Jews, who are also God-fearers" (or "of the Jews and the God-fearers"; the wording is debated). It shows a Jewish community sitting together at the city's public events, and it is one piece of evidence used in the debate over Gentile "God-fearers" (see 18:7). The day-by-day list of islands (Chios, Samos) reads like a ship's log, and the Byzantine text adds a stop at Trogyllium (see the variant).

p: The Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when pilgrims filled Jerusalem. Paul wanted to arrive with the collection.
b: Pentecost (Greek for "fiftieth") is the Feast of Weeks of the Law of Moses (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12), when Jews from many lands came to Jerusalem; Acts 2 sets the coming of the Spirit on this day. Paul was carrying the gift of the Gentile churches (see 20:4). Bringing it at a pilgrim feast would show the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers before the whole Jewish world. Sailing past Ephesus saved days, since a visit there would have involved many farewells and perhaps danger after the riot.

p: The church's leaders are called "elders" here and "overseers" in 20:28. Both words name the same people.
b: "Elders" (presbyteroi) was a familiar title for leaders in Jewish towns and synagogues, and Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in each new church (14:23). In verse 28 Paul tells these same men that the Holy Spirit has made them "overseers" (episkopoi), the word that later became "bishops." So here, as in Titus 1:5–7 and 1 Peter 5:1–2, the two words describe one group. By the time of Ignatius of Antioch (about AD 110), many churches had one overseer (bishop) above a group of elders (presbyters) and deacons. How and when that change happened, and whether it was meant to bind later churches, is one of the main questions dividing the churches (see the card on 20:28). Jerome already noted that in the New Testament elders and overseers were the same (Letter 146).

p: The only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christians. It is a farewell, like those of Moses, Samuel and Jesus.
b: Paul's words at Miletus belong to a well-known type: a leader's farewell before death or departure. Jacob blesses his sons (Genesis 49), Moses gives his last speeches (Deuteronomy 31–33), Joshua and Samuel take leave of Israel (Joshua 23–24; 1 Samuel 12), and Jesus speaks to his disciples at the Last Supper (Luke 22:14–38; John 13–17). Such speeches look back on the speaker's life, warn of dangers ahead, and hand on a charge. Paul does all three. This is also the speech in Acts that sounds most like Paul's own letters, with its appeal to what the hearers "know" (compare 1 Thessalonians 2:1–12).
r: Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 31–33; Joshua 23–24; 1 Samuel 12; Luke 22:14–38; John 13–17; 1 Thessalonians 2:1–12; 2 Timothy 4:6–8

a: I worked as the Lord's slave
t: Serving the Lord as a slave
p: The verb means to serve as a slave. Paul often calls himself Christ's slave in his letters.
b: The Greek douleuō is the verb of doulos, "slave." Paul opens his letters by calling himself a slave of Christ Jesus (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1), and the title echoes the Old Testament "servants" of the LORD such as Moses and David. In a world where many in the church were slaves, the phrase was concrete: Paul belonged wholly to his master. "With all humility" uses a word Paul also uses in his letters for the lowliness that Christ showed (Philippians 2:3; Colossians 3:12; Ephesians 4:2).
r: Romans 1:1; Romans 12:11; Philippians 1:1; Philippians 2:3; Ephesians 4:2; Colossians 3:12

p: Paul taught in public and in homes. The first churches met in their members' houses.
b: There were no church buildings for more than a century. Believers met in homes large enough to hold them. In Ephesus itself, Paul sends greetings from Aquila and Prisca and the church that met in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19). Other house churches are named in Rome (Romans 16:5), Colossae (Philemon 1:2) and Laodicea (Colossians 4:15). Paul's teaching "openly" probably refers to the synagogue and the school of Tyrannus (19:8–9).

p: Paul goes to Jerusalem as one already "bound." Soon he will be bound with real chains.
b: The Greek can mean bound "by the Spirit" (compelled by the Holy Spirit) or "in my spirit" (inwardly determined). The next verse, which names the Holy Spirit, suggests the first. There is also a wordplay: in Caesarea the prophet Agabus ties his own hands and feet with Paul's belt and says the Jews in Jerusalem will bind its owner (21:11), and in Jerusalem the Roman commander orders Paul bound with two chains (21:33). Like Jesus, who turned resolutely toward Jerusalem knowing what waited there (Luke 9:51; 18:31–33), Paul goes forward anyway.
orig: δεδεμένος ἐγὼ τῷ πνεύματι (dedemenos egō tō pneumati)

p: Paul pictures his life as a footrace to be run to the finish line.
b: Athletic games were part of city life across the Greek world, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games. Paul often uses the image: he tells the Corinthians to run so as to win the prize (1 Corinthians 9:24–27), he presses on toward the goal (Philippians 3:14), and at the end he says he has finished the race (2 Timothy 4:7). Luke used the same word for John the Baptist "nearing the end of his race" (13:25). What matters to Paul is not his survival but reaching the end of the task Jesus gave him.

a: you will see my face no more
t: Did Paul ever return to Ephesus?
p: Paul says they will not see him again. The letters to Timothy seem to place him in the area later.
b: Acts never shows Paul back in Ephesus, and Luke repeats this sentence for emphasis (20:38). But 1 Timothy 1:3 has Paul urging Timothy to stay in Ephesus while he went to Macedonia, and 2 Timothy 4:20 says he left Trophimus sick in Miletus, events hard to fit into Acts. Views: (1) Paul was released after the two years of 28:30, traveled again, and did see some of them, so this was his expectation, not a prophecy; (2) Luke wrote after Paul's death and knew this was in fact the last farewell; (3) many critical scholars think the Pastoral Letters were written later in Paul's name, so there is nothing to reconcile. Luke's readers would at least hear the speech as Paul's last words to the church.

a: I am clean of everyone's blood
p: Paul repeats the watchman language from Ezekiel that he used at Corinth.
b: In Ezekiel, God's watchman must warn the wicked. If he warns them, he has saved his own life; if he does not, their blood is on his hands (Ezekiel 3:17–21; 33:1–9). At Corinth Paul said, "I am clean" (18:6). Here he says he has declared "all of God's purpose" (20:27) and warned each of them "night and day" (20:31), so he has done what the watchman must do. The responsibility now passes to the elders, whom he calls to keep watch (20:28, 31).

p: The Greek episkopos is the source of the English "bishop." Here it names the same men called elders in 20:17.
b: Episkopos means "one who looks over, a supervisor." Through Latin episcopus and Old English biscop, it became the English "bishop." The KJV says "overseers" here but "bishop" in 1 Timothy 3:1–2 and Titus 1:7 for the same word, so English readers often do not see that the elders of Ephesus are being called bishops. The verb "to shepherd" in the same sentence gives the English word "pastor" (Latin for "shepherd"), so in this one verse the elders are also called overseers and given the shepherd's task. Churches draw different conclusions from this (see the card).

p: Leaders as shepherds, the church as God's flock: the picture comes from the Old Testament and from Jesus.
b: Israel's Scriptures call God the shepherd of his people (Psalm 23; Psalm 80:1) and blame Israel's leaders as bad shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34). Jesus saw the crowds "like sheep that have no shepherd" (Matthew 9:36), and the risen Jesus told Peter, "Shepherd my sheep" (John 21:16). Peter's first letter gives the same charge to elders (1 Peter 5:2–4). The flock is not the elders' own: it is "the church of God," bought at the highest price.
r: 20:29; Psalm 23:1; Ezekiel 34:1–16; Matthew 9:36; John 10:11–16; John 21:16; 1 Peter 5:2–4

a: which he acquired through his own blood
t: "His own blood" or "the blood of his own"?
p: If God is the subject, does the verse speak of "God's blood"? Or does it mean "the blood of his own Son"?
b: With the reading "the church of God" (see the variant), the Greek dia tou haimatos tou idiou can be read two ways. (1) "Through his own blood": God acquired the church with his own blood, a bold way of saying that the one who died was God the Son. Early Christian writers spoke this way: Ignatius, writing to this same church of Ephesus about AD 110, speaks of "the blood of God" (To the Ephesians 1:1), and Tertullian does likewise. Later theology calls this the "sharing of attributes": what is true of Christ's human nature can be said of the person who is God. (2) "Through the blood of his own one": "his own" may be a title for Christ, as when Paul calls Christ God's own Son (Romans 8:32); the NRSV adopts "his own Son." Bruce Metzger judged it possible that "his Own" was an early title for Jesus. The Plain English Translation says "his own blood" because that is the natural sense of the words and what most English versions print; "the blood of his own Son" is the main alternative. The verb echoes God "buying" his people in Psalm 74:2 and the Greek of Isaiah 43:21.
orig: ἣν περιεποιήσατο διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ ἰδίου (hēn periepoiēsato dia tou haimatos tou idiou)
r: Psalm 74:2; Isaiah 43:21; Romans 8:32; Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9

a: vicious wolves will get in among you
p: Jesus warned of false prophets who are wolves. Paul says the danger will come from outside and from inside.
b: Jesus warned of false prophets who "come to you dressed up as sheep, but underneath they are wolves out for prey" (Matthew 7:15), and sent his disciples out "like sheep into the middle of a pack of wolves" (Matthew 10:16). Ezekiel and Zephaniah call Israel's corrupt officials wolves (Ezekiel 22:27; Zephaniah 3:3). Paul warns of two dangers: wolves who come in from outside, and men from the elders' own ranks (20:30). Later texts show both at Ephesus: false teachers whom Timothy must oppose (1 Timothy 1:3–7, 19–20), and the risen Jesus praising the church for testing those who call themselves apostles (Revelation 2:2).
r: 20:30; Matthew 7:15; Matthew 10:16; John 10:12; Ezekiel 22:27; 1 Timothy 1:3–7; 2 Timothy 1:15; Revelation 2:2; Zephaniah 3:3; 1 Timothy 1:19–20

p: Three months in the synagogue, two years in the hall, and more: about three years by ancient counting.
b: Acts gives three months (19:8), two years (19:10), and "a time" (19:22). Ancient writers often counted any part of a year as a year, so "three years" is a fair total for a stay of about two and a half years, perhaps from AD 52 to 55. Paul's letters from this period speak of hard years there (1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8–10).

a: the inheritance among all who have been made holy
p: In the Old Testament Israel's inheritance was the land. In the New Testament it is a share in God's coming kingdom.
b: The language of "inheritance" goes back to the division of the promised land among Israel's tribes, each receiving its share (Numbers 26:52–56; Joshua 13–19). The New Testament uses the same words for the believers' share in God's future: the inheritance of the saints in the light (Colossians 1:12; compare Ephesians 1:14; Ephesians 1:18). Paul uses nearly the same phrase in his speech before Agrippa (26:18). "Made holy" (sanctified) describes those whom God has set apart as his own, Jews and Gentiles together. The Greek "the one able to build up" could refer to God or to the word; the Plain English Translation, like the Greek, leaves it open.

a: I set my heart on no one's
p: Like Samuel taking leave of Israel, Paul says he took nothing from anyone.
b: Samuel's farewell to Israel asks: "Whose ox did I take? Whose donkey did I take?" (1 Samuel 12:3), and Moses told the LORD, "I have not taken one donkey from them" (Numbers 16:15). Paul's claim fits the farewell type (see 20:18) and his habit of refusing payment from the churches he founded (1 Corinthians 9:12–18; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9; 12:14–18; 1 Thessalonians 2:5–9). Traveling teachers were often accused of greed, so his record mattered. Rich clothing was a form of wealth in the ancient world, which is why he names it with silver and gold.
r: 1 Samuel 12:3–5; Numbers 16:15; 1 Corinthians 9:12–18; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9; 2 Corinthians 12:14–18; 1 Thessalonians 2:5–9; Acts 20:34

t: A saying of Jesus not in the Gospels
p: Paul quotes Jesus with words that appear in none of the four Gospels. Such sayings are called agrapha.
b: None of the Gospels contains this saying, though Luke 6:38 and Luke 14:12–14 say similar things. Sayings of Jesus preserved outside the four Gospels are called agrapha ("unwritten" things). This one is among the most likely to be genuine, since it is in the New Testament itself. Paul also passes on words of the Lord in 1 Corinthians 7:10; 9:14; 11:23–25 and 1 Thessalonians 4:15. Similar maxims circulated among Greeks: Thucydides contrasts a Persian royal custom of giving rather than receiving with a Thracian custom of the opposite (2.97.4). Early Christian writers echo the saying: the church of Rome praises the Corinthians for being "more glad to give than to receive" (1 Clement 2:1).
orig: Μακάριόν ἐστιν μᾶλλον διδόναι ἢ λαμβάνειν (Makarion estin mallon didonai ē lambanein)
r: Luke 6:38; Luke 14:12–14; 1 Corinthians 7:10; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Thessalonians 4:15; 2 Corinthians 9:7

a: he got down on his knees with them all and prayed
p: Jews usually stood to pray. Acts shows Christians kneeling at moments of great need.
b: Standing was the usual posture of prayer for Jews (Mark 11:25; Luke 18:11, 13). Kneeling marked special earnestness: Jesus knelt in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41), Stephen as he died (7:60), Peter beside Tabitha's body (9:40), and Paul again with the believers of Tyre on the beach (21:5). Luke ends the speech not with applause but with prayer.

a: They threw their arms around Paul's neck and kissed him again and again
p: The Greek says they "fell on Paul's neck," the embrace of family reunions and partings in the Bible.
b: The expression echoes Esau, who "fell on his neck and kissed him" (Genesis 33:4); Joseph, who "threw his arms around his brother Benjamin's neck and wept" (Genesis 45:14); and the father in Jesus' parable who ran to his lost son (Luke 15:20). The Greek verb for kissing is a strong, repeated form. The elders' grief shows the bond between Paul and the church he had served for three years.
